title: The enemies within and without
hookLine: the prayer asks for enemies to be ended; many read them also as the five thieves inside

cards: Anandpur, in the last years of the sixteen hundreds. The Tenth Guru's town sits in the hills, and the hills are full of trouble. Neighboring kings resent him.
Imperial armies will later come. There will be sieges, hunger, a night when the town has to be left behind. These aren't metaphors; they're men with weapons, and they're coming.
In this world, the Guru writes a prayer that asks, plainly, for enemies to be ended. It's a line people stumble over when they first read Chaupai.

teach.b: The lines come right after ichhaa. In paraphrase: destroy all my enemies; save me with your own hand. May my family live in peace, and all my servants and Sikhs.

A little later: protect me with your own hand, and end all my foes this very day. The word for enemy here is dusht, the wicked, the one who means harm. Sikhs read these lines in two ways, and they don't have to choose.
The first is the plain one.

The Guru and his community faced real violence, and this is a leader asking God to protect his people from those who would kill them. The tradition doesn't apologize for that; asking for protection from harm isn't hatred.
The Guru Granth Sahib speaks again and again of five thieves in every person: lust, anger, greed, attachment and ego. They live inside the body, the scripture says, and plunder its treasure.
Many Sikhs, saying Chaupai every day, hear the enemies as those five too. The dusht that harms you most on an ordinary Tuesday probably isn't an army.
It's your anger at the driver who cut you off, the greed that keeps you scrolling, the ego that can't say sorry. Notice where the prayer puts the fight.
It doesn't say, let me destroy them. It says, you destroy them, and save me with your hand. The battle, inner or outer, is handed over.
In the prayer's picture, the enemy within doesn't go because it's hated. It goes when the one praying is held by something stronger.

how: Many Sikhs recite these lines of Chaupai Sahib daily, understanding the enemies both as outward threats and as the five thieves: lust, anger, greed, attachment and ego.

o: the wicked one, who means harm
a thief who robs travelers at night
a soldier sent to guard the town

games.q: the enemies within and without — tap the pairs.
p: the wicked, the one who means harm

s: the enemies in Chaupai are only a metaphor
the Guru's community faced real armies. many Sikhs also hear the five thieves inside, and hold both readings.
the Guru Granth Sahib speaks of five thieves in every person
lust, anger, greed, attachment and ego, which plunder the treasure within.
the prayer asks the one praying to destroy the enemies himself
it asks God to destroy them and to save him with God's own hand.

games.q: you're the Guru at Anandpur, with real enemies gathering in the hills. what does your prayer ask for?
o: the strength to destroy them myself.
you destroy my enemies, and save me with your own hand.
games.why: Chaupai hands the fight over: destroy all my enemies, save me with your hand. many Sikhs hear the same request against the five thieves within.

practice: Think of the five thieves, lust, anger, greed, attachment, ego, and without listing all your faults, notice which one has been busiest in you lately, and name it in one word.
Then, instead of fighting it, picture handing it over, the way the prayer does. If you pray, say Waheguru as you do; if not, just let your grip on it loosen a little.

wordCard.voice: Dusht, the wicked. Chaupai's lines asking for enemies to be ended: real armies for the Guru, and for many Sikhs, the five thieves inside too.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: dusht, the wicked or the one who means harm; in Chaupai, the enemies the prayer asks God to end.

carryVoice: Your line: end the enemy within. The fight, inner or outer, is handed over. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: five thieves (panj chor), a recurring image in the Guru Granth Sahib
